**Reasoning**

Electrical current can flow through a material only if it contains mobile charge carriers (free electrons, ions, etc.).  

| Material | Dominant charge carriers | Conductivity (relative) |
|----------|--------------------------|--------------------------|
| **Aluminum** | Free electrons (metal) | Very high – good conductor, used for power lines |
| **Copper**   | Free electrons (metal) | Extremely high – one of the best conductors, standard wiring |
| **Plastic**  | None (no free electrons or ions) | Negligible – an electrical insulator |
| **Water**    | Ions (from dissolved salts/minerals) | Low‑to‑moderate – pure water is a poor conductor, but ordinary water contains enough ions to conduct noticeably |

- **Metals (Al, Cu)** have abundant free electrons, so they conduct electricity readily.  
- **Water** can conduct electricity because dissolved ions provide charge carriers; even “pure” water conducts far better than an insulating polymer.  
- **Plastic** lacks any mobile charge carriers; its electrons are tightly bound within covalent bonds, making it an excellent insulator.

Thus, among the four options, plastic is the material **least likely** to allow electricity to flow.

**Conclusion**

The correct choice is **C**.

**Final answer:** C
